newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian 97/98 cocoa grind over 200,000T - industry.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian 97/98 cocoa grind over 200,000T - industry.

text.p: Ivory Coast's cocoa grind could rise by around 20 percent to around 200,000 tonnes in the 1997/98 season (Oct-Sept) as new capacity comes on stream, industry analysts say.
"That does not include the most recent (factory) announcements as it takes a good year to build a factory," said one.

Commodities Minister Guy-Alain Gauze told Reuters in June that Ivorian grinding capacity could rise to 360,000 tonnes in 1997/98 but local analysts say the figure is too optimistic as most factories take at least a year to build.
Ivory Coast's existing cocoa grinding capacity from four factories stands at 162,000 tonnes although industry analysts expect the total 1996/97 grind to reach just 145,000 tonnes.
One said expansion by existing processors would raise capacity to close to 200,000, with possible processing by oil palm-crushing plants taking the total to just over that figure.
"Some of the (1997/98) light crop (May-Sept) could also be processed (by new factories announced) but we have not taken that into account," said the analyst.
French-Swiss group Barry Callebaut owns three plants under the names of SACO and Chocodi.

"We expect SACO in San Pedro (second largest port) to expand from 20,000 to 30,000 tonnes, and SACO in Abidjan (commercial capital) from 45,000 to 60,000 (in 1997/98)," said the industry source. Chocodi's output would remain the same at 15,000 tonnes -- giving a company total of 105,000 tonnes, he added.
Barry Callebaut chief executive Pierre Vermaut said in June the company wanted to raise capacity in Ivory Coast. Gauze later said the firm's output would rise to 100,000 tonnes.
Abidjan-based UNICAO, partly owned by U.S. based Archer Daniels Midland, has said it will raise its capacity by over 20,000 to 86,000 tonnes by 1998.

Processing by Ivory-based Industrial Promotion Services, which also owns the country's main jute sack maker, FILTISAC, could process around 10,000 tonnes -- which would take the total to over 200,000 tonnes -- but no decision had been taken, the analyst said.
"IPS has talked about using an expeller method to process 10,000 tonnes and they (through a company called Oliatech) did some trials a few years ago at an oil palm plant," he said.
U.S. based commodities group Cargill said on Friday it and Ivorian firm Groupe d'Investissements et de Participations Afrique (GIP) had agreed to form a joint venture for cocoa exporting.
A new cocoa processing plant for processing up to 65,000 tonnes of beans a year was also under consideration, a Cargill Europe statement said on Friday. No firm details were given.

French chocolate firm CEMOI has started building a 50,000 tonnes of beans a year capacity factory near Abidjan and another Franco-Dutch-Ivorian group Orexis told Reuters it has plans, not yet confirmed, to build build a 25,000 tonnes plant in San Pedro.
CEMOI said its plant could be operating in late 1997/98.
Analysts say that could take the overall processing figure well over the 200,000 tonnes-mark but they said few factories took less than a year to build, test and put into full production.
Other unconfirmed factory plans remain on the drawing board.
Ivory Coast wants to process 50 percent of its annual crops, currently running at around 1.1 million tonnes plus a year, by 2000.
-- Abidjan newsroom, + 225 21 90 90
